items.title: Acemoglu and Robinson argue institutions explain development
items.claim: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's 2001 AER paper used settler mortality as an instrument for institutional quality. What did they find?

options.text: Places where European settlement was deadly (tropics) developed 'extractive' colonial institutions; places suitable for settlement got 'inclusive' institutions. Institutional differences persist and explain a large share of cross-country income variation today

items.reveal:
The 2001 AER paper used settler mortality data to instrument for current institutions (since geography affects mortality but, AJR argue, only affects current outcomes through institutions). Their book 'Why Nations Fail' (2012) developed the inclusive vs extractive institutions framework for a general audience.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson won the 2024 Nobel for this body of work. Critics (Glaeser, Sachs) have argued for the role of geography, human capital and culture; the debate over weights between institutional and other factors continues.
items.why: Cross-country growth differences are large and persistent. Identifying causal drivers is genuinely difficult; AJR's instrumental approach was an influential attempt.

items.title: Potential GDP is not directly observable
items.claim: The output gap is actual GDP minus potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential. Why is this concept difficult to use in practice?

options.text: Potential GDP is unobservable — it must be estimated, and estimates are revised heavily after the fact. Pre-2008 estimates of potential GDP have been revised down substantially, suggesting the economy was less overheated than thought
It is observable directly from satellite

items.reveal_title: A concept whose measurement is treacherous
items.reveal:
OECD, IMF and central bank estimates of potential GDP use filters (Hodrick-Prescott, Kalman) and production function approaches. They produce different numbers and revise heavily as data arrives.

Orphanides's 2003 paper showed that real-time output gap estimates available to the Fed in the 1970s were systematically wrong, contributing to policy errors.

The BIS has criticised reliance on output gaps for monetary policy.
items.why: Policy variables that depend on unobservable concepts inherit estimation uncertainty. Output gap-based 'rules' look cleaner in textbooks than in practice.

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.
